planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in fall or early spring in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; pinch stems once or twice in late spring to keep the tall, lax stems from flopping before bloom.

directions: This Great Plains botanical variety of azure sage carries noticeably larger, showier sky-blue flower spikes than the straight species, making it a superior garden form while keeping the same drought tolerance and gray-green narrow foliage. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and resist the urge to fertilize or overwater, since rich conditions encourage weak, floppy growth. It blooms from late summer into fall, pairing beautifully with goldenrod and native asters, and the abundant tubular flowers are a strong late-season draw for bumblebees and migrating pollinators. Cut stems back hard in late winter before new basal growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps need little supplemental water once rooted in.

directions: Nekan is a long-established selection of pitcher sage chosen from wild populations in the Nebraska-Kansas region for its sturdier, more upright habit and heavier production of true azure-blue flower spikes compared to seed-grown plants. It thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy soils and resents heavy, wet clay, making it a good fit for dry, sun-baked Gulf Coast beds rather than low spots. Bloom runs from midsummer into fall and draws bumblebees and other long-tongued native bees in numbers. Cut the woody stems back to the basal rosette in late winter to renew the clump for the coming season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; bulbs multiply readily and are best left undisturbed for years once established.

directions: Native to prairies and open ground from the central Gulf states west into Texas and Mexico, this rain lily sends up a single fragrant white flower, sometimes faintly flushed or veined pink, that opens in late afternoon or evening and lasts only a couple of days per flush. Flowering is triggered by warm-season rainfall events from late spring through fall, so established clumps can bloom in surprise waves after a storm. Plant bulbs in average garden soil that drains well but is not kept bone-dry, and allow the strappy foliage to die back naturally between bloom cycles. Clumps slowly naturalize into sizable colonies at the front of a border or in short native meadow plantings, and the evening blooms are visited by moths and other crepuscular pollinators.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun; give it room, since this selection still reaches full swamp-sunflower height.

directions: Gold Lace is a finely textured selection of swamp sunflower prized for its narrow, lacy dark-green foliage that gives the whole plant a softer, airier look than the species before the flowers even open. In fall it carries the same dense, multibranched flush of small bright-yellow daisies that make swamp sunflower one of the best late-season nectar plants for the Gulf Coast garden. Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun at the back of a border or along a pond margin where its height is an asset rather than a flopping liability. Bees, skippers, and migrating monarchs work the flowers heavily right up to frost, and goldfinches favor the ripened seed heads afterward.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average to moist soil in full sun; unlike the species, this dwarf selection tolerates drier garden conditions and does not need staking.

directions: Low Down is a dramatically dwarfed sport of swamp sunflower, standing little more than knee-high or shorter where the species can reach six to eight feet, which makes it one of the few ways to work this native fall bloomer into a small bed or container without staking. It carries the same cheerful golden-yellow, dark-eyed daisies in a dense, rounded flush from late summer into fall and spreads gradually by rhizome to form a tidy low colony rather than a towering thicket. It performs well in both evenly moist and average garden soil, giving it more placement flexibility than the straight species. Bees and late-season butterflies visit the blooms freely, and the compact habit makes deadheading or cutting back after bloom quick work.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; expect bloom later in the season than most other swamp sunflower selections.

directions: Mellow Yellow was selected from the Louisiana coastal plain for its softer, gentler lemon-yellow flower color, a departure from the more saturated gold of typical swamp sunflower, and for its distinctly late flowering window that can stretch into November when most other perennials are long finished. It reaches full swamp-sunflower stature on rough-textured, threadlike foliage and needs the same consistently moist to wet, acidic soil the species favors along ditches and pond margins. Give it room at the back of a wet border where its height and late display extend the pollinator season for bees and migrating butterflies well past the first light frosts in protected microclimates. Cut stems back after seed heads fade to tidy the planting for winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; settle it into its permanent spot at planting time since established clumps dislike being moved.

directions: Wisley Jester is a Royal Horticultural Society-recognized selection of the native woodland wildflower Indian pink, carrying the same whorled, glossy foliage and upright stems topped with narrow, tubular crimson flowers that flare open to reveal bright yellow star-shaped lobes. It thrives at a woodland edge or shaded border in moist, humus-rich soil, where its late-spring to early-summer bloom draws ruby-throated hummingbirds reliably and swallowtail butterflies occasionally. Like the species it is slow to establish and best left undisturbed once planted, gradually forming a dense clump rather than spreading aggressively. Combine it with ferns, heuchera, or woodland phlox for a shaded native planting with strong hummingbird appeal.
